candidato.titulo: Why exercise has become a key part of cancer treatment
candidato.resumo: Scientists have long known that regular exercise decreases the risk of developing many types of cancer. But last year, results from a large, randomized clinical trial of patients with colon cancer definitively showed what many observational studies and animal research had been hinting at for decades: People who exercise following cancer treatment have a better chance of surviving the disease and a lower likelihood of recurrence.

texto_fonte:
Why exercise has become a key part of cancer treatment
Scientists have long known that regular exercise decreases the risk of developing many types of cancer. But last year, results from a large, randomized clinical trial of patients with colon cancer definitively showed what many observational studies and animal research had been hinting at for decades: People who exercise following cancer treatment have a better chance of surviving the disease and a lower likelihood of recurrence.
Known as the CHALLENGE trial and led by scientists at the University of Alberta and Queen's University in Canada, it showed the benefit of exercise in patients with colon cancer, but observational studies have seen similar boosts to survival in other types of cancer, including breast cancer and prostate cancer.
It's also been clear for a while that exercise can help mitigate many symptoms of cancer or cancer treatment's burdensome side effects as well as improve patients' and survivors' quality of life. But results like those from the CHALLENGE trial have moved physical activity from an add-on into the spotlight together with more traditional cancer treatments, said Allison Betof, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor of medicine (oncology) whose Ph.D. research focused on exercise oncology.
"We've now seen this move from exercise as a quality-of-life recommendation to truly incorporating it into ongoing cancer care with a goal of improving survival," Betof said. More randomized clinical trial results will be needed for other types of cancer besides colon cancer, she said, "but for an intervention that we already know is safe and improves quality of life, it makes sense to get this into the hands of patients as soon as possible."
Betof and other exercise experts at Stanford Medicine offer their insight on what patients and survivors should know about the cancer-specific benefits of working out, how to safely incorporate physical activity into their treatment plans and why they might want to find a cancer rehabilitation expert to support their exercise journey.
1. Exercise is safe for those with cancer—even those in active treatment
Just a few decades ago, it was common advice for cancer patients to rest as much as possible while in treatment. Many cancer therapies are hard on the body, and doctors and other care providers advised patients to take it easy.
"Previously, there was this idea that rest is really needed until treatment is over," said Alyssa Mixon, D.O., a Stanford Medicine physical medicine and rehabilitation physician who specializes in working with cancer patients. "Now, we emphasize that movement is medicine."
That doesn't mean all cancer patients should sign up for their first marathon while completing chemotherapy courses or ignore activity restrictions after surgery, Mixon said. The treatments can be taxing, and patients should listen to their bodies and their doctors. But there's now a good body of evidence that exercise is safe—and beneficial—even during active treatment.
2. Physical activity can supercharge cancer therapies
About those benefits: Animal studies and observational studies in humans suggest that regular physical activity helps boost cancer survival by enhancing the effects of cancer treatments.
In 2015, Betof led a study in a mouse model of breast cancer showing that mice that exercised regularly grew more blood vessels around their tumors and had more oxygen in the tumors, both of which are associated with better prognoses. Animals that exercised had reduced tumor growth, and when the scientists gave them chemotherapy, those that worked out responded better to the drugs.
Other researchers have noted similar treatment-enhancing effects for other types of cancer and other forms of cancer treatment, including surgery, radiation and immunotherapy, a class of cancer therapy that uses the body's own immune system to fight the cancer.
Researchers have also seen that in patients who exercise, certain cancer-fighting immune cells are more active in the bloodstream and around tumors, Betof said, which could explain why working out helps patients fare better.
3. Working out may help alleviate common cancer symptoms as well as treatment side effects
Fatigue is one of the most common symptoms of cancer and a frequent side effect of its associated treatments. It may sound counterintuitive, but research has shown that moving is the best defense.
"While this may not make sense to someone tired from cancer therapy, appropriate exercise has been shown to decrease fatigue," said Anjali Sibley, M.D., a clinical associate professor of medicine (oncology). "Exercise is one of the most effective ways to treat cancer-related fatigue."
A 2017 meta-analysis (a study assessing the findings from many other previous studies) found that regular exercise bested all other methods for combating cancer-associated fatigue, including medications and supplements. Cognitive behavioral therapy and mindfulness exercises are also effective in combating fatigue, studies have shown.
Research also indicates that regular exercise helps cancer patients with other symptoms of their disease or treatment, including boosting their moods, reducing joint pain (a common side effect of aromatase inhibitors, a hormone therapy treatment for breast cancer) and improving overall quality of life, Sibley said.
4. Exercise recommendations for cancer patients and survivors mirror those for the general public—but something is better than nothing
Like those for the general public, guidelines from the American Cancer Society for cancer patients and survivors recommend exercising at moderate intensity for at least 150 minutes a week or intensely for at least 75 minutes a week and adding strength or resistance training at least twice a week. But if those numbers sound intimidating, start where you are able.
"People often think, 'If I'm not going to the gym for 50 minutes, it's not worth going.' And that's not true for patients with cancer," Betof said. "We have shown that minutes per week of exercise is the thing that matters, more so than intensity. A walk is much better than saying, 'I don't feel up to going to the gym so I'm not going to do anything.'"
With the fatigue and stress of the disease and its associated treatments, there may be days or weeks when an intense workout feels out of reach. Those fluctuations should be built into a patient's exercise plan together with their care providers, Sibley said.
"Patients will be able to do different levels of exercise depending on the day or week and depending on where they are in their treatment course," she said. "Some days will allow more vigorous movement while others will encourage lighter movement or temporary pauses."
5. Consider seeking out an expert in cancer and movement
Unlike the general public, however, those with a cancer diagnosis—especially those in active treatment—may want to avoid their neighborhood gym.
Many cancer patients have lowered immunity, so a crowded, indoor space may be risky. Some also have disease-specific needs that the average personal trainer or gym class teacher might not have knowledge of: postsurgery activity restrictions, sensitive skin from radiation treatment or bone or muscle weakness from tumors in those areas, for example.
This is where an expert in cancer rehabilitation can be key, Mixon said. She recently joined Stanford Medicine from the University of Virginia to launch Stanford Health Care's first cancer rehab program.
Along with specialized physical therapists, speech therapists and occupational therapists, rehabilitation physicians like Mixon support cancer patients' physical well-being through a comprehensive therapy plan using a variety of modalities: coordination and supervision of lymphedema therapists for compression wrapping for lymphedema, the accumulation of excess lymph fluid that can be a side effect of certain cancer surgeries; speech therapy for patients whose mouth, throat or vocal cords are affected by their cancers; and physical or occupational therapy to recover after cancer surgeries.
Those with expertise in cancer and exercise can design workout plans for patients that take their specific limitations into account but still give them the benefits of regular exercise, Mixon said.
Unfortunately, not every cancer clinic has a specialized rehab program. Groups like Mixon's are more common within larger, academic health care systems. For those without in-person access, however, several organizations offer online programs and advice.
Some of Stanford Health Care's free cancer wellness classes are available virtually, and the cancer-support nonprofit Livestrong runs exercise programs for cancer patients and survivors through YMCAs around the U.S. and online.
And even where specialized programs exist, not all patients and oncologists are aware of them, Mixon said. She hopes that as more data proving the benefits of exercise like those from the CHALLENGE trial come out, awareness will grow.
"It's never too early or too late to refer a patient to cancer rehab, once they have been diagnosed," Mixon said. "Many patients understand the importance of exercise but might be afraid or concerned about what they should be doing, and that's where having that education from a cancer rehab doctor comes into play."

candidato.titulo: Fish prove every pregnancy is a battle: Unexpected evidence for the food fight between mothers and babies
candidato.resumo: Left to their own devices, babies in the womb would suck their mothers dry. A developing baby benefits from taking as many essential nutrients as possible, but evolutionary theory predicts that to survive pregnancy, mothers need to keep some of these nutrients for themselves.

texto_fonte:
Fish prove every pregnancy is a battle: Unexpected evidence for the food fight between mothers and babies
Left to their own devices, babies in the womb would suck their mothers dry. A developing baby benefits from taking as many essential nutrients as possible, but evolutionary theory predicts that to survive pregnancy, mothers need to keep some of these nutrients for themselves.
New UC Riverside research published in Science Advances has found evidence of this struggle in another part of the animal kingdom. For the first time outside mammals, researchers identified a genetic conflict between mothers and babies in fish with a placenta, suggesting pregnancy itself can create this conflict.
When UCR evolutionary biologist David Reznick first heard the idea, years ago, that mothers and their unborn offspring might have competing interests, he thought it was nonsense. After all, mothers need healthy babies, and babies need healthy mothers. Why would nature pit them against each other?
"I thought it was the silliest thing I'd ever heard," Reznick said. "I rejected the idea out of hand."
Competing interests shape gene activity
The new findings support a theory Reznick once dismissed: that mothers and their developing babies have competing evolutionary interests. Scientists believe this conflict helps explain a process called genomic imprinting. Normally, both parents contribute working copies of genes to their offspring. But for some genes, only the copy inherited from the mother or the father is active, while the other is switched off.
In mammals, the affected genes influence how much nourishment a baby receives, with genes inherited from fathers sometimes encouraging growth and those inherited from mothers restraining it.
Why would genes inherited from mothers and fathers have different effects on a baby's growth? The answer lies in how evolution favors the passing of genes from one generation to the next.
A mother's evolutionary success depends not only on the survival of her current baby but also on her ability to pass her genes to additional offspring. For the developing baby, however, its own survival matters more than the survival of any future sibling.
That's because a baby shares, on average, only half its genes with a full sibling, and even fewer with a sibling who has a different father. Evolution can therefore favor genes that help a baby obtain additional nourishment, even when doing so compromises its mother's ability to have other healthy children.
This isn't simply a struggle over limited food. Providing nourishment to a developing baby requires energy, and giving more to one offspring can leave a mother with less to support herself or future pregnancies. Even if she eventually recovers, the time and energy required may delay her next pregnancy or reduce the number of offspring she produces over her lifetime.
"What's in the best interest of the baby to get from its mother is more than what's in the mother's best interest to give," Reznick said.
The genes behind competing demands
Reznick calls genes that encourage growth and greater demands for nourishment the "give me more" genes, and those that restrain growth the "you can't have it" genes. The father's copy of a "give me more" gene isn't automatically stronger or dominant over the mother's copy, but if the mother's copy is silenced, then the father rules.
Likewise, if the mother's copy of a "you can't have it" gene is active and the father's copy is silenced, then the mother rules. Which parent's copy is active depends on the particular gene.
Why would evolution produce this arrangement? A baby that gets more nourishment may have a better chance of surviving and passing on its genes, including those inherited from its father.
But because the mother's future children could have different fathers, genes from a gestating baby's father likely favor greater demands for nutrients at the expense of any future offspring. Genes from the mother, meanwhile, might favor self-preservation so she can pass her genes to more offspring.
Imprinting doesn't necessarily resolve these competing interests. But it can influence how much nourishment a developing baby receives and keep competing influences from overtaking one another.
Placental fish offer an evolutionary test
Scientists first discovered imprinting in mammals through experiments with mouse embryos and later found it in flowering plants, where mothers also nourish their developing offspring after fertilization.
For Reznick, those discoveries were difficult to ignore. He had spent years studying a family of fish that includes guppies and mollies. Unlike most fish, which lay eggs, all the fish in this family give birth to live young, and some have also evolved placentas that deliver nourishment to their developing babies throughout pregnancy.
Many fish pack all the nourishment their young will need into eggs before fertilization. In species with placentas, however, mothers continue supplying nutrients during pregnancy, creating opportunities for genes to influence how much the developing babies receive.
These fish offered a way to test whether imprinting evolves when mothers and developing babies remain connected through a placenta. Fish and mammals last shared a common ancestor hundreds of millions of years ago, long before either group evolved its modern placenta.
To test the idea, Reznick bred separate fish family lines through 10 to 12 generations of brother-sister matings, then crossed fish from different lines. This allowed researchers to distinguish genes inherited from mothers and fathers in the resulting offspring.
Collaborators from the comparative genomics laboratory led by Xu Wang at the Auburn University College of Veterinary Medicine examined genetic activity in the developing fish's placental tissue, looking for cases in which one parent's copy of a gene was more active than the other's.
Shared patterns across distant species
They found patterns of gene activity consistent with the competing maternal and paternal interests predicted by evolutionary theory. The finding of imprinting in fish suggests that this mechanism may have evolved independently in animals that developed placentas millions of years apart.
Fish and mammal placentas also appear to use some of the same groups of genes to move nutrients into cells. Despite evolving their placentas independently, both groups seem to have arrived at some of the same biological solutions.
The findings could also shed light on human pregnancy. Errors in imprinting are associated with developmental disorders, and understanding why certain genes are active or silent may help scientists better understand how fetal growth is controlled.
For Reznick, the results represent a remarkable change of heart. The evolutionary struggle between mothers and their developing babies, which he once dismissed as nonsense, now appears to extend far beyond mammals.
"We like to think there's something special about mammals," Reznick said. "But it turns out these aren't such special features."
Publication details
Ying Zhang et al., Independent origin of genomic imprinting in placental fish, Science Advances (2026). DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh5487

candidato.resumo: E se um robô pudesse construir sozinho uma estrutura no espaço, sem precisar da ajuda de astronautas? A ideia pode parecer digna de um filme de ficção científica, mas já aconteceu: no início do mês, a agência Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) construiu uma estrutura no espaço com um robô . Para a missão Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA) , a agência usou um “construtor” composto por um manipulador autônomo, que coleta hastes e juntas armazenadas por perto. Depois, o equipamento monta seções idênticas para criar uma treliça perimetral. O resultado foi uma antena refletora de 1,4 m feita de filme Kapton, tubos de fibra composta e juntas de alumínio. texto_fonte:
Parece ficção científica, mas aconteceu: robô da DARPA constrói antena sozinho no espaço
Por Danielle Cassita |
E se um robô pudesse construir sozinho uma estrutura no espaço, sem precisar da ajuda de astronautas? A ideia pode parecer digna de um filme de ficção científica, mas já aconteceu: no início do mês, a agência Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) construiu uma estrutura no espaço com um robô.
Para a missão Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA), a agência usou um “construtor” composto por um manipulador autônomo, que coleta hastes e juntas armazenadas por perto. Depois, o equipamento monta seções idênticas para criar uma treliça perimetral. O resultado foi uma antena refletora de 1,4 m feita de filme Kapton, tubos de fibra composta e juntas de alumínio.
Claro que a ASTRA foi uma demonstração, ou seja, foi conduzida para os pesquisadores verificarem onde o processo precisava de ajustes e identificar obstáculos antes de tentar algo mais ousado. Deu certo: a equipe já se deparou com limitações de tempo, que não permitiram que eles construíssem seções adicionais da antena. Mesmo assim, os resultados permitiram concluir esta que foi a terceira fase de um projeto da DARPA.
Construção no espaço
Futuramente, o objetivo da DARPA é ir além com seu programa Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design, ou apenas “NOM4D”. "O objetivo do NOM4D é viabilizar a construção eficiente e escalável de estruturas de grande porte no espaço", disse Andrew Detor, gerente do programa, em um comunicado.
E, por “grande porte”, ele se refere a estruturas na escala de centenas de metros ou, por que não, de quilômetros. “Nada próximo dessa escala pode ser feito hoje”, observou. Já Sergio Pellegrino, engenheiro civil e aeroespacial, destacou o potencial de projetos do tipo não somente para a astronomia e astrofísica, mas também para a comunicação e outras áreas, “como a construção de painéis solares bem grandes para energia solar espacial”, sugeriu.
Se tudo correr bem, Pellegrino acredita que robôs podem construir espelhos ainda maiores de telescópios, que permitiriam que os observatórios estudassem objetos ainda mais distantes no espaço, bem como estruturas avançadas para radiotelescópios.

candidato.titulo: Siri AI Developer Preview Lets iOS, iPadOS, and macOS Apps Integrate with Siri
candidato.resumo: Apple released the Siri AI Developer Preview in the 27.3 beta releases of its operating systems, enabling developers and apps to integrate with the assistant and hand off actions to it. During the Preview, access to Siri AI is restricted to developer builds and internal TestFlight testers. By Sergio De Simone

texto_fonte:
Apple released the Siri AI Developer Preview in the 27.3 beta releases of its operating systems, enabling developers and apps to integrate with the assistant and hand off actions to it. During the Preview, access to Siri AI is restricted to developer builds and internal TestFlight testers.
Apple says that Siri AI is an entirely new version of its assistant which is "profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal".
Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more.
These new capabilities let users make natural language requests and have Siri AI carry out any custom action supported by the app. The framework also supports complex requests through Skills, a new feature that lets developers "teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience".
If a request does not specify an app name, it will automatically be routed to the app currently in the foreground, the app associated with an active Live Activity, or the app previously mentioned in the ongoing conversation. This allows users to continue conversations across an app and its Live Activity, or a different app altogether. While an app is running in the background, however, it will receive only requests that explicitly mention its name.
Requests can also include actions across apps, such as finding content in one app, sending it to another, and perform an action there.
Commenting on Apple's announcement, Reddit user sixtypercenttogether noted:
In my limited testing so far it does what it says. If you include a good description on your intent and parameters, Siri can figure it out. THIS is what Siri should have been all along, all the way back in 26.0.
User Medical_Lengthiness6 compared Apple's approach to integrating Siri AI to Google's AppFunctions:
Doing it via app intents was the right move. Google could have done this with the android intents but instead decided to make a completely different agent skills sdk that you have to implement.
All Apple Intelligence features, including Siri AI, may be subject to usage limits, with extended, premium access planned the future. Finally, developers besed in the EU should be aware that Siri AI is currently unavailable in the EU on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS.

candidato.titulo: Unannounced Intel Core Ultra 7 260K CPU surfaces in Newegg prebuilt gaming PCs
candidato.resumo: The mysterious Intel Core Ultra 7 260K has surfaced in some prebuilt gaming PCs on Newegg, despite no official mention of the chip from Intel.

texto_fonte:
A new Intel Arrow Lake SKU is listed for sale in multiple prebuilt PCs on Newegg, despite no official acknowledgement of the model from Intel. The Core Ultra 7 260K is a downclocked version of the Core Ultra 7 265K from Intel's main Arrow Lake stack, not the Arrow Lake Refresh stack that's infiltrated our list of the best CPUs for gaming. Outside of a few prebuilt listings on Newegg's website, you'll find no mention of the CPU elsewhere online (including Intel's official Core Ultra Series 2 specs page).
Although retailer-exclusive and late-generation variants are common from AMD and Intel — we recently reviewed the Ryzen 5 5500F, for instance — they almost never fly completely under the radar, as is the case with the Core Ultra 7 260K. The chip itself is identical to the Core Ultra 7 265K based on the specs we know, fitted with 20 cores, eight of which are P-cores. The 260K tops out at 5.4 GHz, however, while the 265K reaches 5.5 GHz.
Otherwise, the specs are all the same. It comes with the same 125W TDP, same 30 MB of L3 cache, and same support for up to 256 GB of memory running at DDR5-6400. We only know of these specs from an image shown on the two ABS prebuilt listings available with the 260K. It's available in the ABS Kaze II paired with an RTX 5060, as well as the Flux II Aqua with an RTX 5070.
The image is below, captured hastily, as you can see, from a Microsoft Teams call. Again, we weren't able to find any information from Intel about the chip outside of this slide.
One critical detail this slide confirms is that the Core Ultra 7 260K belongs to the Arrow Lake family, not the range of Arrow Lake Refresh processors like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus. It tops out at DDR5-6400, while Arrow Lake Refresh climbs up to DDR5-7200. That means the chip doesn't have access to the hardware-level enhancements available in Arrow Lake Refresh, nor the software-based Intel Binary Optimization Tool that boosts performance in select games.
Although that's enough to categorize the 260K, there are some details that are unclear. In the two PCs it's available in, the chip is referred to as the 260K across the full product page except in Newegg's option selector (pictured below), where it's referred to as the U7-260KF. Intel's KF models are unlocked for overclocking but lack integrated graphics.
Additionally, the slide from Intel referenced above shows the chip boosting up to 5.4 GHz, but the product page lists the chip at 5.2 GHz for maximum boost clock.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Newegg has told us that the chip is exclusive to the retailer and will only be sold through its in-house ABS prebuilts. ABS machines are normally sold with components Newegg already sells piecemeal, offering a convenient way to get a full rig with parts you can identify. The ABS Flux II Aqua, which is available with the chip, is on sale at Newegg now for $300 off.
The ABS Flux II Aqua gaming PC comes with an Intel CPU, an Nvidia GeForce GeForce RTX 5070 graphics card, a 1TB NVMe SSD with Gen 4 speeds, and 32GB of DDR5-6000 RAM. This is a 1440p gaming powerhouse with the potential for 4K.
We've reached out to Intel to get more details about the Core Ultra 7 260K, and we'll update this story when we hear back. Although the specs suggest the 260K should perform almost identically to the 265K, we haven't had a chance to test the CPU ourselves. And, as you can see from the rankings in our CPU benchmark hierarchy, we recommend most Intel shoppers move toward an Arrow Lake Refresh SKU.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

candidato.titulo: Gemini and DECam showcase a young Type Ia supernova
candidato.resumo: A star's explosive demise has added a shiny new feature to NGC 1433, a barred spiral galaxy approximately 50 million light-years away in the southern constellation Horologium (the Pendulum Clock). New images of supernova SN 2026ahvu from the U.S. Department of Energy–fabricated Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and the Gemini South telescope capture the explosion against its galactic surroundings, recording an event that is changing in appearance from night to night.

texto_fonte:
Gemini and DECam showcase a young Type Ia supernova
A star's explosive demise has added a shiny new feature to NGC 1433, a barred spiral galaxy approximately 50 million light-years away in the southern constellation Horologium (the Pendulum Clock). New images of supernova SN 2026ahvu from the U.S. Department of Energy–fabricated Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and the Gemini South telescope capture the explosion against its galactic surroundings, recording an event that is changing in appearance from night to night.
DECam is mounted on the U.S. National Science Foundation Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile, a program of NSF NOIRLab. Gemini South is one half of the International Gemini Observatory, an international collaboration led by the NSF, in partnership with Canada, Chile, Brazil, Argentina, and the Republic of Korea, and operated by NSF NOIRLab.
The Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System (ATLAS) discovered the object on Nov. 2, 2026. Initially designated AT 2026ahvu, it was subsequently confirmed through spectroscopy to be a young Type Ia supernova—an explosion of a white dwarf that has accreted matter from a close companion star—and received the designation SN 2026ahvu. At discovery, its apparent magnitude was approximately 17; within days, observations reported it at magnitude 13.5.
The supernova, visible in the image above to the right and slightly below the galaxy's center, is expected to reach a maximum brightness of magnitude 10.5–12.1 between Nov. 18 and 23. Its discovery well before reaching peak brightness, combined with its relative proximity, gives astronomers the rare and valuable opportunity to witness the early development of the explosion and gather evidence that can quickly disappear as the expanding debris evolves. This is one of the nearest Type Ia supernovae observed since SN 2011fe was discovered in the Pinwheel Galaxy (Messier 101) in 2011.
Type Ia supernovae arise from the thermonuclear destruction of white dwarfs, the dense remnants of stars like our sun. Although astronomers use these explosions to measure cosmic distances, important questions remain about the stellar systems that produce them and precisely how they ignite. Observations during the earliest stages can help distinguish between possible explosion scenarios and search for signs of interaction with a companion star or surrounding material.
DECam also captured images of NGC 1433 before the explosion during observations for the Dark Energy Survey (DES), a survey led by DOE's Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, conducted from 2013 to 2019, to investigate the nature of dark energy. DECam's images allow astronomers to compare the supernova's environment pre- and post-explosion. Combined with the sharper Gemini imaging that provides a more in-depth view of the system, these observations demonstrate how combining NOIRLab facilities enables deeper investigation into rapidly changing phenomena in the night sky.
NOIRLab is coordinating follow-up observations with Blanco/DECam, Gemini, and the Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) Telescope on Cerro Pachón in Chile. Combining these facilities gives astronomers a more complete picture of the supernova.
Repeated imaging tracks how its brightness and color evolve, while spectroscopy shows what the expanding material is made of and how fast it is moving. By following the explosion from its first days through its peak brightness and into its long fade, researchers can learn about the system before it exploded and the mechanism of the explosion. Together, these clues help astronomers refine Type Ia supernovae as a tool for measuring the expanding universe.
Telescopes on the ground and in space are already turning their attention to SN 2026ahvu. NOIRLab invites other observatories to contribute complementary observations that would extend coverage across wavelengths and time zones. Coordinating these efforts can capture changes that any single facility might miss and help astronomers maximize what can be learned from this nearby explosion.
The event is also within reach of amateur astronomers. At its reported brightness, SN 2026ahvu can already be seen in small to moderately sized amateur telescopes under favorable conditions, particularly from southern locations where NGC 1433 rises high in the sky. To the eye, the supernova appears as a faint point of light, offering observers the chance to witness the changing glow of an exploding star in another galaxy.
The new DECam and Gemini images capture one moment in that unfolding story. Over the coming weeks, observations from professional and amateur astronomers will help trace its evolution, gathering clues to the physics of stellar explosions and the cosmic distance markers that help us measure our universe.

candidato.titulo: Research advances quantum computing that harnesses speed of light
candidato.resumo: Quantum computers have the potential to perform calculations more quickly than supercomputers, but they could be even faster and more energy-efficient if they were built with photons as their basic units, called qubits.

texto_fonte:
Research advances quantum computing that harnesses speed of light
Quantum computers have the potential to perform calculations more quickly than supercomputers, but they could be even faster and more energy-efficient if they were built with photons as their basic units, called qubits.
Challenges remain, however, in fabricating the chips that allow photons to function as qubits in circuits. Purdue University engineers have developed potential solutions to several major issues with building these chips, known as quantum photonic integrated circuits, on a large scale.
A qubit is a quantum version of a "bit" that a conventional computer uses to process information as zeros and ones. Whereas bits can only take the state of zero or one at a time, a qubit represents both zero and one simultaneously through a phenomenon called superposition, greatly expanding the amount of information processed.
Photons, the smallest possible particles of light, have several advantages over other quantum particles that could be used for building qubits. For example, individual photons would enable qubits to move through the gates of a circuit at the speed of light, transferring data faster and minimizing delays in algorithm performance. Since photons aren't easily disturbed by heat or other changes in their surroundings, they can also offer qubits stability at room temperature. Other types of qubits require supercold temperatures to operate, consuming more energy.
Quantum photonic integrated circuits can work with a small number of qubits, but to perform practical calculations, quantum computers would need hundreds if not thousands of qubits, a scale that is not yet possible with these chips.
"Single photons are the building blocks of quantum photonics. The biggest challenges in scaling up a quantum photonic integrated circuit have to do with creating good single-photon sources," said Vladimir Shalaev, the Bob and Anne Burnett Distinguished Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering.
Shalaev and Alexandra Boltasseva lead work in Purdue's Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Birck Nanotechnology Center and the Purdue Quantum Science and Engineering Institute on key challenges with building quantum photonic integrated circuits. Their past discoveries on how to manipulate light on the nanoscale have been foundational to the fields of photonics and optics. For multiple years, they have each been recognized on the Clarivate Highly Cited Researchers list for work ranking in the top 1% of citations in the Web of Science.
Boltasseva, the Ron and Dotty Garvin Tonjes Distinguished Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering, also was featured on last year's Quantum 100 list as part of the United Nations-designated International Year of Quantum Science and Technology.
A more reliable way to produce single photons
One of the difficulties with building a quantum photonic integrated circuit is generating one photon at a time to take the form of a qubit.
In 2021, Shalaev and Boltasseva published a study in Science Advances demonstrating a way to emit single photons using silicon nitride, a material that has become the industry standard for constructing quantum photonic platforms.
But the process the industry has been using for photon emission, called spontaneous parametric down-conversion, generates single photons inconsistently and with low efficiency.
The method Shalaev and Boltasseva's team developed emits exactly one photon at room temperature from dozens of locations on a silicon nitride platform every time a laser beam shoots through it.
The sources of photon emission are modifications to atomic structure, called "defects," that the researchers created within the platform. These atomic defects limit light emission to a single photon at a time.
Shalaev and Boltasseva have also since shown in a study presented at the 2022 Conference on Lasers and Electro-Optics that they can control the placement and number of defects by embedding them in nanosized pillars on the silicon nitride platform, which would allow the platform to be manufactured more uniformly for use in a quantum photonic integrated circuit.
A single-photon switch
Another issue Shalaev and Boltasseva are tackling is that single photons don't readily interact with each other, making them hard to control on a chip using switches.
In a conventional computer, switches called transistors toggle bits between zero and one states to process information. Similarly, switches in a quantum photonic integrated circuit would enable photons to act as qubits.
Shalaev and Boltasseva's research team reported in a Nature Nanotechnology paper last year that they built a switch capable of operating on the level of single photons.
The proof-of-concept switch adapts a mechanism that the industry has used to modulate light with another high-intensity light beam for applications such as fiber-optic communications. This mechanism, called optical nonlinearity, allows a "control" light beam to interact with a "probe" beam but at power levels that would be too high to work with single photons.
With the Purdue-developed method, a single photon from the control beam strikes silicon, creating an electron that then triggers an avalanche of electrons. This avalanche alters how light passes through a material, which also changes its refractive index, a property that controls light propagation. Changing silicon's refractive index allows the probe beam to pass through the device only when a single photon starts the electron avalanche process, effectively allowing the photon to switch the beam on and off.
A tool for predicting quantum decoherence
Even though qubits based on photons would be less affected by their surroundings, a single disturbance could still cause qubits to fall out of superposition or entanglement, creating errors in a quantum computer's calculations.
This kind of disturbance is called decoherence. Purdue electrical and computer engineering professor Alexander Kildishev and Purdue graduate student Pranshu Maan led a team that included Shalaev and Boltasseva in demonstrating an approach that could make it possible to prevent decoherence by anticipating it before it happens. The team published findings in Nature Communications in May this year.
"Decoherence is seemingly random, but in fact there is a certain pattern that can be recognized. This study takes an important step in identifying such a pattern using machine learning," Boltasseva said.
The team found through statistical-physics analysis that the way decoherence happens over time presents a pattern. They then used machine learning to validate that these patterns have information that could be predicted. The researchers turned these components into a framework that learns and could anticipate the dynamics of a quantum system, which would then enable proactive control of decoherence rather than only responding to it after it occurs.
With this framework, the researchers demonstrated a way to predict and reduce one of the major causes of decoherence, called spectral diffusion. This phenomenon happens when an emitted photon shifts across the electromagnetic spectrum due to disorder that naturally happens in the surrounding environment, changing the photon's frequency and therefore its energy level. Because superposition only works if all photons in a quantum system are indistinguishable from one another, a change in a single photon's energy level would cause superposition to fall apart.
The researchers discovered that spectral shifts retain a memory of how an emitted photon's frequency has wandered over time, revealing a predictable temporal pattern. The team developed an algorithm with a built-in memory mechanism and trained it on data from individual quantum emitters to predict future spectral shifts. Using these predictions, they showed that an anticipatory-control approach could reduce spectral shifts by as much as 20-fold in the quantum systems studied.
Just being able to predict decoherence could have a big impact on a quantum computer's performance.
"You can't get rid of decoherence—it's the law of nature that everything fluctuates. But if you recognize the pattern of decoherence and learn how to control it, then you can minimize it," Shalaev said.
"Let's say you need a hundred qubits to run a quantum algorithm, but typically far more than that, say 10,000 qubits, to deal with errors caused by decoherence. If I minimize those errors somehow, then the number of qubits needed to run my algorithm would also be minimized."
In principle, this approach could lay the foundation for making it possible to anticipate decoherence across multiple quantum systems, which is needed for building the scalable quantum architecture that quantum computers would use. Those predictions could then be combined with active tuning to keep different emitters more closely aligned, improving the indistinguishability and synchronization of the photons they generate.
Next, the team plans to use tools from statistical physics to extract the hidden properties of a quantum system's fluctuating environment from its measured dynamics. These physical insights will be incorporated into machine-learning models to improve their ability to predict decoherence. The team will also investigate whether the models can identify the microscopic processes responsible for spectral shifts, with the long-term goal of predicting and suppressing decoherence before it significantly disrupts the quantum state.
Publication details
Pranshu Maan et al., Anticipating decoherence in quantum systems, Nature Communications (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-72829-3

texto_fonte:
Minimum PC game system requirements are damn near useless. Sure, they’ll tell you what hardware you need to get a game running, but whether it’ll actually run well is anybody’s guess. Valve is finally doing something about it, putting real-world performance data on Steam store pages so gamers can see what frame rates other people are getting before plunking down their hard-earned cash, starting with the Steam Deck.
Valve is pushing Steam beyond Windows and conventional PCs. Figuring out how games will run on all that new hardware is another headache entirely.
Valve announced this week that Steam now displays average frame rates for thousands of Steam Deck games, collected anonymously from players who opt in to sharing performance data (“a majority of Steam Deck players”). You’ll find the numbers under Steam Deck Compatibility > Learn more on supported store pages, alongside an expandable histogram showing how frequently games hit different frame rates. Verified, Playable, and even Unsupported games are included.
As Ars Technica notes, Cyberpunk 2077 and Skyrim: Special Edition both carry Steam Deck’s coveted Verified badge, but player data shows the former typically hovering around 30 to 40 fps while the latter cruises along at 50 to 60 fps. Even Assassin’s Creed Syndicate, officially Unsupported, approaches 60 fps on Steam Deck OLED. Compatibility badges aren’t designed to measure frame rates alone, of course, but that’s exactly why these newly surfaced numbers can be so helpful. The histogram shows how performance samples are distributed rather than burying everything beneath a single average. Valve doesn’t normalize individual graphics settings, and none of this replaces proper frame-time analysis, but I’ll take actual performance data over a vague badge any day.
After months of brutal supply headaches, the 512GB Steam Deck OLED now costs $789, while the 1TB model skyrocketed to a pearl-clutching $949. That’s $240 and $300 more than before, respectively, for the same hardware. Taking your existing PC game library anywhere remains a fantastic proposition. Swallowing those prices is in a nightmare year for the PC is something entirely different.
Steam’s bigger performance play
PCWorld’s Michael Crider reported back in April that Valve was giving developers access to real-world Steam Deck performance information, and he practically begged the company to put those numbers on store pages. Wish granted!
Mike also spotted evidence of something even more ambitious lurking in Steam’s code: a frame-rate estimator designed to predict how games perform on specific PC hardware configurations.
Valve explicitly calls the new Steam Deck charts a “stepping stone toward providing framerate data for more devices than just Steam Deck,” and it’s already asking desktop Steam beta users to contribute anonymized frame-rate data. If you’ve ever tried to figure out whether a hot new game will run decently on your particular PC’s CPU and GPU combo, you instantly understand how useful that could be. Generic system requirements rarely tell you anything, and finding benchmarks for something resembling your setup can be an utter crapshoot.
Getting reliable estimates from desktop PCs is a much nastier problem than collecting Steam Deck numbers. Steam Decks have set hardware configurations like game consoles do. But two gaming rigs with identical CPUs and GPUs can perform wildly differently depending on resolution, graphics settings, upscaling, drivers, and memory configurations. It’s been an impossible egg to crack thus far, but Steam has millions of gamers running practically every hardware combination imaginable, with the software needed to collect performance information already installed.
Developers obviously test their games, but Valve could eventually build something they can’t easily replicate: a continuously updated picture of how those games perform on the messy frankensteined-together masses of PCs that people actually own. Pull it off, and Steam might finally tell you something useful about how a game will run on your PC before you buy it.
Further reading: Valve escaped Windows. Now Steam is breaking free of the PC itself.

candidato.titulo: Gemini 4 Hydrogen é o novo modelo do Google para tarefas do dia a dia
candidato.resumo: Novo modelo substitui o Gemini 3.8 Flash e chega gratuitamente ao aplicativo Gemini e à Busca do Google. Gemini 4 Hydrogen é o novo modelo do Google para tarefas do dia a dia

texto_fonte:
Resumo IA
- Google lançou o Gemini 4 Hydrogen, um modelo de inteligência artificial focado em tarefas cotidianas, que substitui o Gemini 3.8 Flash e oferece respostas 2,5 vezes mais rápidas.
- O Gemini 4 Hydrogen está disponível gratuitamente no aplicativo Gemini e na Busca do Google, e oferece preços de API de US$ 1,50 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 7,50 por milhão de tokens de saída para desenvolvedores.
- O modelo teve bom desempenho em testes de localização e correção de código, mas ficou atrás do Claude Sonnet 5.5 em tarefas de operação de sistemas e na resolução de problemas científicos e matemáticos.
O Google anunciou nesta quinta-feira (12/11) o mais um novo modelo de inteligência artificial, dessa vez voltado a tarefas cotidianas. O Gemini 4 Hydrogen substitui o Gemini 3.8 Flash, prometendo respostas 2,5 vezes mais rápidas e melhorias de precisão.
O modelo já começou a ser disponibilizado no aplicativo do Gemini e na Busca do Google, inclusive para não assinantes. Já desenvolvedores que pretendem incorporá-lo a apps e serviços próprios, a API segue os seguintes preços:
- Tokens de entrada: US$ 1,50 por milhão
- Tokens de saída: US$ 7,50 por milhão
O acesso está disponível por meio das ferramentas de integração do Google, incluindo o Google AI Studio e o Android Studio.
Modelo básico faz frente ao Gemini 4 Argon
O Hydrogen combina velocidade, capacidade de raciocínio e menor custo de operação frente aos outros modelos da família, segundo o Google. Mesmo sendo mais indicado para produção de textos e tarefas comuns, nota-se que o modelo básico conseguiu bons resultados em algumas atividades.
No Artificial Analysis Intelligence, índice independente que reúne diferentes testes para medir a capacidade de modelos de IA, o Hydrogen alcançou 51 pontos na configuração padrão e bateu 54 com o nível máximo de raciocínio, contra 50 do Gemini 4 Argon.
Frente ao Gemini 3.8 Flash, o Gemini 4 Hydrogen também reduziu a ocorrência de alucinações em mais de cinco vezes, além de ser 2,3 vezes mais resistente a ataques de prompt injection.
Contra modelos concorrentes, como o Claude Sonnet 5.5, da Anthropic, e o GPT-6.1 Terra, da OpenAI, os resultados mostram algumas vantagens, como:
- Localização e correção de projetos de software (SWE-sweep)
- Automatização de tarefas profissionais e administrativas (AutomationBench-AA e Agents Last Exam v1.1)
- Interpretação de documentos (Multimodal Knowledge Agent [MKA])
O desempenho muda quando a avaliação exige operação de sistemas e resolução de tarefas científicas e matemáticas. O modelo do Google ficou atrás do Claude Sonnet 5.5 em testes como Terminal-Bench 4.1, Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 e no benchmark que avalia a interatividade do modelo com o computador, OSWorld-2.1, um dos testes mais relevantes para IAs agênticas.
Google integra Hydrogen e Carbon em fluxos de trabalho
O novo modelo básico pode ser integrado ao Gemini 4 Carbon, em um mesmo fluxo de trabalho pela nova ferramenta Orchestrator. A ferramenta funciona de forma semelhante ao comando /swarm, adicionado ao Google Antigravity no lançamento do modelo de fronteira.
A ideia é que o Carbon fique reservado para atividades mais complexas, enquanto o Hydrogen assume etapas que podem ser concluídas com menos recursos. Segundo testes divulgados pelo Google, a combinação apresentou taxas de sucesso próximas às obtidas pelo Carbon Sozinho no Terminal-Bench 4.0, reduzindo o consume do tokens em 24% e o tempo em 19%.

texto_fonte:
Google lança modelo de IA veloz e eficiente; conheça o Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Por Viviane França |
O Google anunciou o Gemini 4 Hydrogen, novo modelo de inteligência artificial desenvolvido para acelerar tarefas de programação e fluxos de trabalho executados por agentes de IA. Com foco em velocidade e eficiência, ele pode funcionar sozinho ou em conjunto com o Gemini 4 Carbon e o Gemini 4 Argon, modelos focados em atividades que exigem raciocínio mais complexo e de longo prazo.
Segundo Koray Kavukcuoglu, vice-presidente sênior do Google DeepMind e arquiteto-chefe de IA do Google, o Hydrogen assume tarefas que precisam de execução rápida, e o Carbon e Argon cuidam das demandas mais complexas. No Google Antigravity, o recurso Orchestrator gerencia essa divisão e alterna entre os modelos durante uma mesma sessão.
Em testes com o Terminal-Bench 4.0, o sistema alcançou resultados próximos aos do Carbon, com 24% menos consumo de cota e conclusão das tarefas 19% mais rápida. O Carbon também pode coordenar vários agentes Hydrogen, responsáveis pela execução e verificação de alterações em ambientes isolados.
O Hydrogen oferece quatro níveis de raciocínio (low, medium, high e xhigh), que definem a quantidade de processamento dedicada a cada tarefa. No Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, marcou 51 pontos no nível high, acima dos 50 do Argon, e chegou a 54 pontos no xhigh. Na configuração padrão (high), é 2,5 vezes mais rápido que o Gemini 3.8 Flash. O desempenho em programação também melhorou: o modelo alcançou 57% de sucesso no Terminal-Bench 4.1, contra 18,2% da versão anterior, e reduziu em mais de cinco vezes a ocorrência de respostas com informações inventadas.
Com janela de contexto de até 1 milhão de tokens de entrada e 1 milhão de tokens de saída, o modelo processa PDFs, planilhas, áudios e vídeos. Também extrai informações de arquivos enviados e serviços conectados, como Gmail, Google Drive, Airtable e Dropbox. No aplicativo Gemini, aciona ferramentas e habilidades adequadas com mais frequência e segue instruções de tom e formato ao longo de conversas com várias interações.
O Google também destaca melhorias de segurança. Em comparação com o Gemini 3.8 Flash, o Hydrogen reduziu em até 81% as ações que ultrapassam as instruções recebidas e em até 79% as tarefas executadas abaixo do esperado. A ocorrência de ações desalinhadas com os objetivos caiu 12 vezes.
Segundo o Google, 99,9% do processo de raciocínio do modelo é legível. Uma auditoria com mais de 200 mil interações também confirmou que não houve edições enganosas na cadeia de raciocínio. O Hydrogen ainda demonstrou ser mais de 2,3 vezes mais resistente a ataques de injeção indireta de comandos no benchmark Gray Swan IPI. No HealthBench Pro, menos de 0,4% das perguntas médicas e científicas receberam recusas indevidas.
O lançamento também inclui mudanças na Busca do Google, disponível globalmente. A ferramenta ganha respostas mais visuais, aprimoramento de consultas para encontrar mais links relacionados e melhor interpretação de perguntas com várias partes, erros de digitação e solicitações específicas.
No Google Sheets, o Gemini gera modelos financeiros interativos mais de 30% mais rápido que os modelos anteriores. Os resultados aparecem no canvas da ferramenta e se ajustam a diferentes cenários de previsão. O recurso está disponível a partir dos planos Google AI Pro e Ultra, incluindo assinaturas corporativas elegíveis.
Como acessar o Gemini 4 Hydrogen?
O Gemini 4 Hydrogen está disponível no aplicativo Gemini e na Busca do Google. No plano gratuito, o aplicativo seleciona o modelo automaticamente, de acordo com a solicitação. Nos planos pagos, o modelo pode ser escolhido no seletor de modelos. Já a integração com o Google Sheets atende aos assinantes dos planos Google AI Pro e Ultra.
Já os desenvolvedores podem utilizar o modelo pela API Gemini, no Google AI Studio e no Android Studio. Os assinantes dos planos Google AI Pro e Ultra também encontram a novidade no Google Antigravity. O preço da API é de US$ 1,50 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 7,50 por milhão de tokens de saída.
No ambiente corporativo, o Hydrogen está disponível no Gemini para Empresas, tanto pela API quanto pelo seletor de modelos. A ferramenta também chegou ao Google Antigravity e ao Gemini para Google Sheets, neste último caso para assinaturas corporativas elegíveis.

candidato.titulo: Tesouro Nacional alerta para vazamento de dados pessoais e chaves Pix
candidato.resumo: Secretaria do Tesouro Nacional identificou um incidente no portal e-Serviços. O ataque expôs dados cadastrais de 30 mil pessoas e 4 mil chaves Pix. Tesouro Nacional alerta para vazamento de dados pessoais e chaves Pix

texto_fonte:
Resumo IA
- O Tesouro Nacional informou que 30 mil usuários do portal e-Serviços tiveram dados cadastrais expostos, incluindo nome, CPF e e-mail.
- 4 mil chaves Pix vinculadas a pagamentos do Governo Federal também foram expostas, mas sem confirmação de comprometimento das contas associadas.
- A STN notificou o incidente à Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados e indicou o serviço Fala.BR para esclarecimento de dúvidas.
A Secretaria do Tesouro Nacional (STN), órgão vinculado ao Ministério da Fazenda, emitiu um alerta para um incidente de segurança que resultou no vazamento de dados de 30 mil usuários do portal e-Serviços, bem como na exposição de 4 mil chaves Pix de pessoas que recebem ou receberam pagamentos do Governo Federal.
O e-Serviços é uma plataforma online da STN que funciona como uma central de atendimento do Tesouro Nacional para esclarecimento de dúvidas, suporte técnico e outras ações. O e-Serviços é usado principalmente por servidores públicos federais, representantes de estados ou municípios e profissionais de contabilidade.
Os dados vazados das 30 mil pessoas incluem nome de usuário, número de CPF e endereço de e-mail.
Já as 4 mil chaves Pix estavam cadastradas em uma base de dados que o Governo Federal acessa para realizar pagamentos a pessoas e empresas. Note, porém, que a exposição dessas chaves não significa que as contas bancárias ou de pagamento associadas a elas tenham sido comprometidas.
Como a invasão aos sistemas da Secretaria do Tesouro Nacional ocorreu?
Essa informação não foi revelada publicamente até o momento. A STN apenas informou que o incidente foi identificado e mitigado em 4 de novembro de 2026. O órgão também esclareceu que o ataque não provocou perdas financeiras ou comprometeu outros de seus sistemas.
Apesar disso, a divulgação do incidente serve para alertar pessoas físicas ou jurídicas que acessam o e-Serviços sobre o risco de contatos ou ações fraudulentas viabilizadas pelos dados vazados.
Seguindo a legislação atual, a STN notificou o incidente de segurança à Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD).
A STN indica o serviço Fala.BR para esclarecimento de dúvidas sobre o vazamento de dados.
Caixa também teve vazamento de dados
A Secretaria do Tesouro Nacional não foi a única instituição pública federal a ter tido um problema de segurança digital recentemente. Outro vazamento de dados afetou clientes da Caixa Vida e Previdência. Esse incidente foi bem mais grave, pois envolveu informações de pelo menos 7,6 milhões de pessoas.
